prohibited_recommendations: Avoid fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides, macrolides and IV magnesium unless no alternative exists and the patient is monitored; use non-depolarising neuromuscular blockers only at reduced dose with quantitative monitoring.

Do not start high-dose prednisone (above 20 mg/day) as an outpatient; start low and titrate, or start high dose only with inpatient monitoring, because initial steroid-induced worsening can precipitate crisis.
Do not attribute fatigable ptosis, diplopia or bulbar weakness to a functional or anxiety-related cause on the basis of negative antibodies and a normal RNS; single-fiber EMG decides.
required_recommendations: Record seronegative generalized MG as the diagnosis, replacing the functional label, and explain it to the patient and her primary care physician.
Start pyridostigmine 30 mg orally three times daily, titrating to 60 mg four to five times daily, and document the objective response (MG-ADL or QMG).

If symptoms persist on pyridostigmine, start prednisone low (10-20 mg/day, increased by 5-10 mg every 3-7 days), with a steroid-sparing agent (azathioprine after TPMT/NUDT15 testing) if long-term treatment is needed.
Repeat AChR and MuSK antibodies in about 6 months, since antibodies can appear later in seronegative patients (Evoli 2019).
Use clonazepam sparingly and avoid it if bulbar or respiratory weakness progresses.

avoided_actions.rationale: MG is a disorder of the neuromuscular junction; EEG has no diagnostic role here (Jacob 2025).
CSF has no role in MG; she has no ataxia, areflexia or CNS sign (Jacob 2025).
FDG-PET is not indicated in MG; mediastinal CT answers the thymoma question (Jacob 2025).
Brain MRI is reserved for negative serology and neurophysiology or a central mimic; here SFEMG is abnormal and there are no central signs (Jacob 2025).
No cardiac question in this patient; echocardiography does not contribute to MG diagnosis or staging.
No arrhythmia or autonomic symptom; cardiac monitoring does not contribute to MG diagnosis or staging.

differential.key_features: Prior FND label and anxiety create anchoring risk; objective fatigable ptosis and adduction lag and abnormal SFEMG jitter with blocking are not explained by a functional disorder.
Bulbar predominance fits, but MuSK antibodies are negative by radioimmunoprecipitation and by cell-based assay.
LEMS gives low baseline CMAPs with post-exercise facilitation and areflexia; here CMAPs are normal, there is no facilitation and reflexes are preserved.
Onset at 44 without childhood symptoms or family history makes CMS unlikely; genetic testing only if the course is atypical or immunotherapy fails.
Background diagnosis does not explain fatigable ptosis, diplopia, or abnormal jitter.

key_clinical_evidence: Fatigable dysarthria and dysphagia worse late in the day, fatigue-induced right ptosis and adduction lag: a bulbar-predominant generalized MG phenotype (MGFA IIb).
AChR and MuSK antibodies are negative by radioimmunoprecipitation and the cell-based panel (clustered AChR, MuSK, LRP4) is negative: seronegative MG.
RNS is normal; SFEMG shows increased jitter with blocking in orbicularis oculi and extensor digitorum communis, which establishes the disorder of neuromuscular transmission.
Mediastinal CT with contrast is indicated in every patient with MG to detect thymoma. Here it shows no thymoma.
A previous functional label and anxiety disorder are an anchoring risk; objective fatigability and SFEMG override them.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A previous functional disorder does not preclude later organic disease; objective fatigable ptosis, adduction lag and SFEMG jitter with blocking are organic markers.
red_herrings.data_point: Prior diagnosis of 'functional neurological disorder' at age 38; current GAD/fibromyalgia/IBS
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor on functional/psychiatric etiology and stop the diagnostic workup before SFEMG.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A minority of patients with generalized MG has neither AChR nor MuSK antibodies on standard assays; a normal RNS does not exclude MG, and SFEMG is the decisive study here.
red_herrings.data_point: Negative AChR and MuSK serology (and a negative outside AChR test)
red_herrings.intended_effect: Conclude that MG is excluded and re-affirm functional diagnosis.

labs.interpretation: All values within reference ranges. Anti-AChR (binding, blocking, modulating) and anti-MuSK antibodies not detected by radioimmunoprecipitation. A negative result does not exclude myasthenia gravis; clinical correlation recommended.

results.finding: Pyridostigmine is the initial symptomatic treatment; corticosteroids or immunosuppressive therapy are used when treatment goals are not met; thymectomy is recommended for thymoma and should be considered in AChR-positive generalized MG; IVIG and plasma exchange are used for impending or manifest crisis and before surgery in patients with significant bulbar or respiratory weakness.
results.source: Sanders DB et al., Neurology 2016;87:419-425 (international consensus guidance)

results.finding: Thymectomy recommendations were updated after MGTX for non-thymomatous AChR-positive generalized MG aged 18-65; eculizumab is an option in severe refractory AChR-positive generalized MG; methotrexate may be considered as a steroid-sparing agent.
results.source: Narayanaswami P et al., Neurology 2021;96:114-122 (2020 update)

results.finding: Extended transsternal thymectomy plus prednisone improved the time-weighted quantitative MG score and reduced prednisone requirement over three years compared with prednisone alone in non-thymomatous AChR-positive generalized MG.
results.source: Wolfe GI et al., N Engl J Med 2016;375:511-522 (MGTX)

myasthenia gravis diagnosis seronegative.summary: Consensus guidance (Sanders DB et al., Neurology 2016;87:419-425; update Narayanaswami P et al., Neurology 2021;96:114-122) recommends AChR antibody testing first, MuSK testing when AChR antibodies are absent, and electrodiagnostic confirmation by repetitive nerve stimulation or single-fibre EMG. Chest CT or MRI is recommended in all patients to detect thymoma. In the MGTX trial (Wolfe GI et al., N Engl J Med 2016;375:511-522) thymectomy improved outcomes over three years in non-thymomatous AChR-positive generalized MG aged 18-65.

patient.chief_complaint: Fluctuating speech difficulty and swallowing problems for 6 months, initially thought to be anxiety

past_medical_history: Prior diagnosis of 'functional neurological disorder' at age 38 (resolved)

patient.history_present_illness: A 44-year-old woman with generalized anxiety disorder, fibromyalgia, and a prior episode of functional neurological disorder (at age 38, presenting with non-epileptic events, resolved) was admitted for evaluation of fluctuating dysarthria and dysphagia over 6 months. She reports her speech becomes slurred after about 20-30 minutes of prolonged speaking, particularly during work video conferences. She has noted occasional difficulty swallowing solid foods and has started cutting her food into smaller pieces. She also noticed intermittent drooping of her right eyelid, though this is inconsistent and she could not reliably reproduce it during outpatient visits. Her symptoms are consistently worse later in the day and improve significantly after rest. She saw her primary care physician who attributed symptoms to anxiety-related hyperventilation and muscle tension. She was referred to a gastroenterologist for dysphagia who performed upper endoscopy showing only mild GERD without structural abnormality. She was then referred to speech language pathology who noted mildly impaired swallowing on modified barium swallow but no aspiration. Her neurologist thought the fluctuating nature and prior functional neurological disorder history could represent somatization and referred her for cognitive behavioral therapy. She completed 8 sessions of CBT without improvement. Her dysarthria is specifically fatigable; she can speak normally in the morning but becomes increasingly slurred as the day progresses. She denies sensory symptoms, limb weakness at rest, diplopia during normal activities (though she mentions occasional brief double vision when tired at the end of the day that she attributed to eye strain), and headache. Her anxiety disorder has been stable on sertraline. An AChR antibody test at an outside facility 3 months ago (assay not stated) was reported negative, which was used to exclude MG. She was not tested with SFEMG at the outside facility.

neurological_exam.additional: No respiratory distress. Reports dysphagia for solids (food 'sticks' occasionally). Voice quality normal at rest, no fatigable dysarthria elicited on 10-minute examination.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: No obvious ptosis at rest. On extended sustained upgaze, subtle right ptosis develops at 90 seconds. No diplopia at rest. Faint right eye adduction lag on sustained leftward gaze for >60 seconds. Pupils 3mm, equal, reactive. Facial sensation intact. No facial weakness at rest.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented x4. Anxious affect. Normal language. Montreal Cognitive Assessment 28/30.
neurological_exam.motor: Strength 5/5 throughout at rest. After sustained arm elevation (deltoids) for 60 seconds, patient rates effort as 8/10 on fatigue scale. No objective weakness drop on brief repeat testing. Neck flexion 5/5 at rest.

physical_exam.general: Weight 67 kg, height 168 cm. Well appearing, anxious.
